confidence_why: Rose 2019, Rose 2022, de Carvalho & Rose 2018 and the acoustic study of Gordon & Rose 2019 all describe the same left-to-right iambic, which surfaces as penultimate stress after rhythmic syncope, and Rose 2014's plain statement that stress falls on the penult is the surface form of that same rule; the only caveat is that every description rests on Rose's fieldwork.

catalog_quote: After word formation, the underlying representation is assigned a syllable structure with only open syllables. Iterative iambic footing starts from the left edge, and the final foot must not align with the right edge of the word. As a result, the last syllable is left unfooted in words with an odd number of syllables, and the last two syllables are left unfooted in words with an even number of syllables. Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot, and rhythmic secondary stresses on other feet ... This means primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the underlying representation in words with an odd number of syllables, and on the antepenultimate syllable in words with an even number of syllables. ... This results in stress occurring regularly on the surface penultimate syllable of words with an iambic parse and regular syncope application, even though stress is not compiled from …
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title (Rose 2019 PDA; Gordon & Rose 2019 ICPhS) are about word stress in Mojeño Trinitario, were already held, and were re-read: both confirm the catalog's 'fixed-unreviewed' coding (L-to-R iambic parse on the underlying CV string, final syllable never strong, primary stress on the rightmost foot = surface penult in regular words, minor trochaic lexical class). HAL/Crossref title queries turned up four further items not in the list of works with stress in the title: de Carvalho & Rose 2018 (LIAMES, downloaded from HAL, §3.4.2 pp.21-22 restates the same system first-hand and adds that a secondary accent is often perceived on the first foot; confirms), Rose 2014 reduplication chapter (Brill, downloaded from HAL, p.377-378: surface penultimate stress with a minority antepenult class and extrametrical classifier/reduplicant suffixes; confirms), Faust 2022 IATL talk (no file on HAL; precursor of the held Faust 2023 Glossa reanalysis, which confirms; low priority), and a 2026 HAL video version of the JIPA Illustration (no stress content in its abstract; none). Nothing read contradicts or supersedes Rose 2019 as the deciding source; no reclassification suggested.1.

new_statements.reading: Fixed, metrically computed stress: left-to-right iterative iambs over the underlying all-open-syllable word with the final syllable (or final two, in even-syllable words) unfooted; primary stress on the rightmost foot, i.e. underlying penult (odd) or antepenult (even), which after rhythmic syncope surfaces as regular penultimate stress; a minor lexical class (101 of 1187 roots) takes a trochaic L-to-R parse, still with rightmost-foot primary stress. Confirmed first-hand by the co-authored diachronic account (de Carvalho & Rose 2018 §3.4.2 pp.21-22, newly downloaded this search of works with stress in the title), the instrumental study (Gordon & Rose 2019) and the JIPA Illustration (Rose 2022); the older surface statement (Rose 2014 p.377: 'Stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable') agrees.

new_statements.quote: Stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable. Only a minority of CVCVCV roots are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable. Most instances of suffixation do not alter the principle of stress placement, that is to say stress automatically shifts to the right, to the penultimate syllable. [p.377] … This process is probably the result of historically rhythmic stress on every even-numbered syllable. In the synchronic system, stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. There are a few lexical exceptions to this rule, and certain suffixes lie outside the stress domain, i.e. they are extrametrical. [p.378]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog and the existing statement: the existing statement already cites this very passage ('Rose 2014 p.377: Stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable') as the surface generalisation of the iambic system, and the catalog rule string (penult in odd-count, antepenult in even-count underlying words) is the underlying parse that surfaces as regular penult after rhythmic syncope. The chapter adds detail the catalog does not record: the extrametricality of stem-internal suffixes (classifiers, reduplicant) with resulting surface antepenult, the minority antepenult root class, and the diachronic remark on rhythmic even-syllable stress. Caveat on identity: the open copy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Surface word stress is regularly penultimate in the prosodic word (the domain of stress, vowel deletion and morphophonology); stress shifts rightward under suffixation to stay penultimate. Stem-internal suffixes (classifiers, the reduplicant) are extrametrical, so when one of them occupies the penult the stress surfaces on the antepenult (p.381: 'When the penultimate syllable of the word is a classifier or red, stress therefore falls on the antepenultimate'); on regular roots 'the position of stress is calculated as if the copy were absent' (p.386). The author explicitly connects the rhythmic vowel-deletion pattern to a historically rhythmic stress on every even-numbered syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the only rhythmic remark is diachronic ('historically rhythmic stress on every even-numbered syllable', p.378). Footnote 7 (p.381): 'Stress is not systematically noted in this paper.'
new_statements.exceptions: (a) 'Only a minority of CVCVCV roots are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable' (p.377); 'a few lexical exceptions' (p.378); fn.2 p.377: 'Some irregularly-stressed roots resist vowel deletion.' (b) Classifiers and the reduplicant are 'normally excluded from the stress domain', giving antepenultimate surface stress when they sit in the penult (p.381, ex. 7); 'Stress can fall on a classifier (9) only on irregular stems with antepenultimate stress such as (8)' (p.381); the copy 'can be stressed on irregularly stressed roots, like kémtone in (24)' (p.386).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes the Trinitario dialect of Mojeño specifically ('the Trinitario dialect of Mojeño, an Arawak language spoken in the Bolivian lowlands', p.375), i.e. the catalog's variety trin1274. The listed citation (Rose 2014, Lenguas de Bolivia III sketch) and the opened file (Rose 2014, Brill reduplication chapter, doi 10.1163/9789004272415_015) are two different 2014 publications by the same author on the same variety; the file read is the latter.

tone_statements.quote: Duration and F0 are less reliable diagnostics for stress, showing considerable interspeaker variation and failing to reliably distinguish three degrees of stress. The inconsistent role of F0 and duration in signalling word stress potentially owes to interference from independent prosodic effects: preboundary lengthening of unstressed vowels in the case of duration and the reservation of F0 as a cue to pitch accent or phrase boundaries [1].

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement. The only apparent tension is one of representational level: the catalog stress on syllable 2 of 3, 2 of 4, 4 of 5, 4 of 6, 6 of 7, 6 of 8 places stress on the penult of odd-syllable words and the antepenult of even-syllable words, which is the underlying (pre-syncope) iambic parse of Rose 2019, whereas Rose 2014 (the reduplication chapter) describes the surface outcome, regular penultimate stress with a minority antepenult root class and extrametrical stem-internal suffixes. The existing catalog statement already reconciles these ('after rhythmic syncope surfaces as regular penultimate stress') and explicitly says the 2014 p.377 sentence agrees. A bibliographic mismatch should be corrected in the record: the citation names the Lenguas de Bolivia sketch (pp. 59-97) but the DOI and the open copy belong to the Brill reduplication chapter (pp. 375-399); the sketch has no open copy (HAL halshs-01211566 lists no file).

sources.quote: Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot. The default parse is an iambic rhythmic pattern that applies to the underlying form of words, which is made up of open syllables only. Words are parsed from left to right by binary iambs, and the last syllable is extrametrical. The language shows another (minor) metrical parse, found exclusively with disyllabic roots (and a handful of exceptional trisyllabic roots), and only when they are bare or carrying post-root morphology only [...]: this trochaic parse applies also from left to right, and the last syllable is not extrametrical.

tone.quote: The Mojeño Trinitario phonological/prosodic word is defined as the domain of stress, rhythmic syncope and phonotactics. [...] Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot. The default parse is an iambic rhythmic pattern that applies to the underlying form of words, which is made up of open syllables only. Words are parsed from left to right by binary iambs, and the last syllable is extrametrical. [...] There is considerable variability on an inter- and intraspeaker basis in the correlates of stress. Preliminary results indicate that the most robust acoustic correlate of word-level stress is intensity, while duration and F0 are less reliable diagnostics for stress (Gordon & Rose 2019).

tone.quote: Duration and F0 are less reliable diagnostics for stress, showing considerable interspeaker variation and failing to reliably distinguish three degrees of stress. The inconsistent role of F0 and duration in signalling word stress potentially owes to interference from independent prosodic effects: preboundary lengthening of unstressed vowels in the case of duration and the reservation of F0 as a cue to pitch accent or phrase boundaries [1].
tone.says: Word prosody analysed purely as metrical stress: intensity is the most robust correlate distinguishing primary/secondary/unstressed vowels; F0 and duration are unreliable stress cues, F0 being attributed to post-lexical prosody ('pitch accent or phrase boundaries', i.e. intonation). No lexical tone is posited (Trinitario).

sources.quote: Trinitario main accent falls on the last foot, whatever the metrical parse [...] Trinitario shows a default iambic rhythmic parse that is entirely consistent with the default stress pattern of the Ignaciano variety. The rhythmic pattern applies to the underlying form of words, posited as being constituted by a succession of open syllables. Words are parsed from left to right by binary iambs, that is, Prosodic Feet with a weak-strong pattern, and the last syllable is extrametrical, as shown in (5). Just as in Ignaciano, disyllabic nouns (and a few trisyllabic nouns like ˈsorare 'animal' [...]) are accented on the first syllable. (p.21)

sources.quote: This video presents the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet for the phonological system of Mojeño Trinitario, an Arawak language spoken in Bolivia. (HAL abstract)
